problemText: Read this sentence from a story: 'The dog barked loudly when the mailman arrived at the gate.' Which part of this sentence is an EXPLICIT statement?
choices: The mailman felt scared by the dog's reaction because we must infer the mailman's emotions from context clues in the story.
The dog was protective of its owner's house based on what we can understand about the dog's behavior and purpose.
The dog barked loudly when the mailman arrived at the gate.
The dog had been trained to guard the property as shown by details we can figure out from the text.
hints: An explicit statement uses plain words that are written right there in the text.
Look for a fact you can point to word for word, with nothing to figure out.

problemText: Read this passage: 'Yuki had studied the spelling list every night for a week. On test day, she wrote each word carefully and checked her work twice before turning in her paper.' Which statement is an INFERENCE, not something the text states directly?
choices: Yuki studied the spelling list every night for a week.
The spelling test happened on a day Yuki had prepared for.
She checked her work twice before turning in her paper.
Yuki wanted to do well on the spelling test.
hints: An inference is something the text does not say in plain words but that you figure out from the details.
Look for a statement about what Yuki was thinking or feeling, not just what she did.

problemText:
A student read this passage and made the claim below. Is this claim an inference supported by textual evidence, or is it just restating something the text already says explicitly?

Passage: 'Kai arrived at soccer practice with his shin guards already on and his cleats laced tight.'

Student's claim: 'Kai arrived at soccer practice ready to play right away.'

Which is true?
choices: It is a valid inference because no sentence in the passage says Kai was ready to play.
It is just a restatement because the passage already says Kai had his shin guards on and cleats laced.
It is a guess because the passage does not explain why Kai wore his gear.
It is an assumption because being ready to play requires knowledge about soccer that the passage does not teach.
hints: Check whether any sentence in the passage uses the exact words 'ready to play.'
An inference combines details the text gives to reach a new conclusion; a restatement just rewrites what was already said.

problemText:
Read this passage, then decide which statement is a valid inference with proper textual evidence.

Passage: 'The library's new computer lab had been closed for three weeks. When it finally opened on Monday, there was a line of twenty students waiting at the door before the librarian unlocked it. By Wednesday, the computers were all taken up during lunch period, and a sign-up sheet had to be posted.'

Which inference below is best supported by evidence from the text?
choices: Students are not interested in using computers at school because they did not sign up for the scheduled time slots.
Students had been waiting to use the new computer lab and wanted to access it as soon as it became available.
The library ordered new computers because the old ones were broken and could no longer support student use.
The librarian decided to close the lab because too many students were using it at once and needed to manage access.
hints: Look for details showing student behavior and what those details suggest about student interest.
Point to the exact phrases that prove your answer: what did students do when the lab opened, and what does that tell you about how much they wanted it?

problemText:
A student read this passage and wrote an inference. Read both, then decide if the inference needs to be fixed because it includes information from outside the text.

Passage: 'Every afternoon at three o'clock, Mr. Chen locked his classroom door and walked to the gymnasium. He always carried a stack of clipboards and a whistle. The gymnasium was where students gathered for practice after school.'

Student's inference: 'Mr. Chen coaches a school sports team because he is athletic and loves to exercise.'

What should the student do to fix this inference?
choices: Change 'coaches' to 'works with' because the passage does not use the word coaches to describe Mr. Chen's role.
Remove the phrase 'a school sports team' because the passage never mentions a specific sport or team name.
Remove the phrase 'because he is athletic and loves to exercise' because those ideas come from outside the passage, not from its details.
Keep the entire inference but add supporting details about Mr. Chen's personality traits because the clipboard and whistle prove he must be someone who enjoys physical activity and fitness.
hints: An inference can only use details the passage itself provides; 'athletic' and 'loves to exercise' are not mentioned in the text.
Check whether the text actually says anything about why Mr. Chen does what he does, or whether the student added an outside belief.

problemText:
Read this passage, then answer the question that follows.

Passage: 'Jamila skipped her usual route through the park and took the long street instead. When she passed the old community center, she slowed down and stared at the colorful construction sign: NEW YOUTH CENTER OPENING NEXT MONTH. That evening, she spent two hours looking at the center's new website, clicked through every photo of the art studio, dance studio, and music room, and saved three pages of information in a folder.'

A reader makes this inference: 'Jamila is interested in the activities at the new youth center.' Which one of these is the BEST textual evidence to support that inference?
choices: Jamila took a long street instead of her usual route through the park, which shows she changed her normal behavior that day.
The construction sign said the center would open next month and displayed colorful information about the upcoming facility.
The youth center has an art studio, a dance studio, and a music room available for students to use.
She spent two hours looking at the website, clicked through every photo of the studios, and saved three pages of information.
hints: Look for the evidence that shows Jamila's own behavior and choices, not just facts about the building itself.
The strongest evidence shows what Jamila did with her time and attention, not just what exists at the center.

problemText: A story has four sentences. Sentence 1 tells us that a girl named Rosa always wears a red scarf. Sentence 2 describes what Rosa has for lunch. Sentence 3 explains that Rosa's red scarf gets caught in a door. Sentence 4 shows how Rosa uses her quick thinking to free the scarf before it tears. Which sentence is a setup for Sentence 4?
choices: Sentence 2, because it describes what Rosa ate and happens right after Sentence 1 in the story
Sentence 1, because it introduces the red scarf earlier in the story
Sentence 3, because it directly comes before Sentence 4 and shows the scarf getting caught
Sentence 4, because it is where the problem gets solved and the payoff happens
hints: A setup is a detail placed early that a later moment depends on.
Ask yourself: what detail from an earlier sentence does Sentence 4 need to make sense?

problemText: Read this short story: Sentence 1: 'Marco had never been inside a library before, and the first thing he noticed was how quiet it was.' Sentence 2: 'He whispered his question to the librarian instead of speaking out loud.' Sentence 3: 'The librarian smiled and helped him find a book about building model airplanes.' Sentence 4: 'Marco left carrying the book, already planning to come back.' What does Sentence 1 do for the rest of the story? A student says, 'Sentence 1 is at the beginning of the story.' Explain why that answer does not describe Sentence 1's job, and then tell what its actual job is.
choices: It comes before all the other sentences and establishes the beginning part of the narrative
It tells us that Marco is in a new place at the start of the story
It establishes that the library is quiet, which is why Marco whispers instead of speaking out loud in Sentence 2
It summarizes Marco's first impression of the library without connecting to later events
hints: Naming where a sentence sits in the story is a location, not a job.
Look for a detail from Sentence 1 that explains why Marco acts a certain way in Sentence 2.

problemText: A student reads this story and is asked how Sentence 2 fits into the overall structure: Sentence 1: 'Chen's little brother had accidentally knocked over a pitcher of juice on the kitchen table last week.' Sentence 2: 'Chen decided to keep a roll of paper towels on a shelf at the corner of the table, within easy reach.' Sentence 3: 'The next afternoon, Chen's brother spilled his cup of apple juice again.' Sentence 4: 'This time, Chen grabbed the roll from the shelf and cleaned it up before any juice dripped onto the floor.' The student answers: 'Sentence 2 is a setup for Sentence 4.' Is this answer correct? Why or why not?
choices: Yes, because Sentence 2 comes after the first spill and before the second spill happens
No, because Sentence 2 only describes where Chen put the paper towels, not why he put them there
No, because Sentence 3 is the real setup for Sentence 4 since it describes the second spill
Yes, because Sentence 2 places the paper towels where Chen needs them, and Sentence 4 shows Chen using them
hints: A setup is correct when you can point to a later moment where that detail actually pays off.
Ask: in Sentence 4, what detail from Sentence 2 does Chen's quick cleanup depend on?

problemText: Read this story: Sentence 1: 'Every time it rained, puddles formed at the bottom of the school playground slide because the ground was not level.' Sentence 2: 'Nobody complained about the puddles or asked the principal to fix them.' Sentence 3: 'One rainy Tuesday, a kindergartner slipped at the bottom of the slide and scraped her knee badly.' Sentence 4: 'The next week, the principal had the ground graded and the puddles stopped forming.' A student must explain what Sentence 1 does and what Sentence 2 does, and how they work together. The student says: 'Sentence 1 is the setup and Sentence 2 is more setup that makes the problem worse.' Is this correct? Why or why not? If it is not correct, explain what each sentence actually does.
choices: No. Sentence 1 sets up the puddle problem, but Sentence 2 sets up the reason the problem stays unfixed long enough for Sentence 3's accident to happen
No. Sentence 1 describes a dangerous condition and Sentence 2 explains why no one prevented the accident, so they work together to make Sentence 3 inevitable
Yes, they are both descriptions of the situation at the playground that come before Sentence 3 and therefore qualify as setup sentences
Yes, both sentences are setup because they both describe the problem and its causes before the accident in Sentence 3
hints: A setup does work for the ending only if you can point to a later moment where it pays off.
Ask: what does Sentence 3's accident need from Sentence 1? What does it need from Sentence 2?

problemText: A story is building toward a theme about how small acts of honesty can spread: Sentence 1: 'Kenji found a wallet with fifty dollars in the grass near the park bench.' Sentence 2: 'He spent an hour looking for the person's phone number and called to return it.' Sentence 3: 'The owner, Mrs. Lin, was so grateful that she told the story to her book club.' Sentence 4: 'At the next book club meeting, three of Mrs. Lin's friends announced they would return lost items they had been holding onto for years.' Which sentence sets up the information that Sentence 4 depends on, and why does that detail matter to the story's overall point about honesty spreading?
choices: Sentence 1, because it introduces the wallet Kenji finds
Sentence 2, because it shows Kenji's honest choice, which Mrs. Lin later tells others about in Sentence 3
Sentence 3, because it explains how Kenji's honesty reaches Mrs. Lin's friends through the book club
Sentence 4, because it shows the final result of the chain of honesty
hints: The theme is about honesty spreading, so ask what honest action has to happen for the rest to follow.
For Sentence 3 to make sense, Mrs. Lin needs to have a story to tell. Where does that story come from?

problemText: A student reads this story and claims that Sentence 2 has no job in the overall structure: Sentence 1: 'In her new apartment, Jen noticed that the kitchen light flickered whenever anyone used the coffee maker.' Sentence 2: 'She called the landlord twice about the flickering light, but he said there was nothing wrong with it.' Sentence 3: 'One morning before a big presentation, Jen brewed coffee and the light went out completely, leaving her apartment dark.' Sentence 4: 'She grabbed her laptop and walked to a coffee shop two blocks away where the power was working.' The student argues: 'Sentence 2 is just a summary of what Jen did. It does not set up anything for the ending because Sentence 1 already told us the light flickered.' Evaluate this claim. Is the student correct? If not, explain what job Sentence 2 actually does and prove it by pointing to a later sentence where that job pays off.
choices: The student is correct; Sentence 2 is only a summary of Jen's action and does not affect what happens later
The student is incorrect because Sentence 2 is about calling the landlord, not about the light itself, so it must serve a different function than Sentence 1

The student is incorrect. Sentence 2 sets up the fact that the problem was never fixed by the landlord, which is why the light fails completely in Sentence 3, making Sentence 4's alternative solution necessary
The student is correct because Sentence 3 mentions the light going out, not the landlord's response, so Sentence 2's information does not lead to the payoff
hints: A summary restates what happened. A setup plants a detail that a later moment depends on to make sense.
Ask: if you removed Sentence 2, would Sentence 3's complete failure still read as inevitable, or would it feel like bad luck?

problemText: Which of the following best describes what the exposition stage of a plot does?
choices: Settles the conflict and shows what things look like after the turning point
Shows the moment when the outcome of the story finally becomes decided
Describes a series of complications that build tension after a conflict starts
Introduces the characters, setting, and situation before any conflict appears
hints: Look for the stage that comes first in the plot's order.
Think about what 'ordinary situation' means — what happens before trouble starts?

problemText: Read this sentence from a story: 'When the storm finally hit the ship, the crew held tight to the railings as waves crashed over the deck, and nobody knew if they would make it to shore.' Which plot stage does this sentence belong in, and why?
choices: Rising action, because the outcome is still uncertain and tension is building
Exposition, because it introduces the main characters and the setting where the story takes place
Climax, because the storm has arrived and the crew must now face the worst part of their struggle
Resolution, because it concludes the story by showing the crew's final destination and what they learned
hints: Ask yourself: has the trouble started, and is the outcome still unknown?
The crew's fate is still uncertain — they don't know if they will make it. What stage describes this uncertainty?

problemText: A student is reading a story and encounters this sentence: 'The old dog limped across the yard and lay down under the oak tree, exactly as she had done every afternoon for ten years.' Is this sentence most likely part of the exposition, rising action, climax, or resolution? Explain your reasoning.
choices: Rising action, because the dog's limp indicates an injury that will cause conflict later in the story
Exposition, because it describes an ordinary, repeated routine before any trouble appears
Climax, because the dog's daily action under the tree marks the moment of greatest tension in the narrative
Resolution, because the sentence shows how the dog spends her final years and what becomes of her afterward
hints: Notice that nothing has gone wrong yet — this is a peaceful, daily habit.
Which stage sets up the normal situation before trouble starts?

problemText: Read this three-sentence passage: 'Marcus had been practicing skateboard tricks in the park for two months, hoping to impress his friends at the competition. During his first run, his board flew out from under him and crashed into the judge's table. Marcus picked up his cracked board and walked off the course while his friends groaned.' Sort these sentences into their plot stages and explain how you know where the rising action ends and the climax begins.
choices: Rising action: first sentence only. Climax: second sentence. Rising action continues through the third sentence as a result.
Exposition: first sentence. Rising action: second sentence. Climax: third sentence because that is when Marcus leaves.
Exposition: first sentence. Rising action: second sentence. Resolution: third sentence because the outcome is now decided.
Exposition: first and second sentences together. Climax: third sentence because that is the most stressful moment.
hints: Which sentence introduces the ordinary situation before trouble? Which one contains the turning point where the outcome becomes clear?
The crash decides the outcome — Marcus will not win. The third sentence shows what happens after that decision.

problemText: A student labeled this sentence as the climax: 'The principal walked into the classroom and the entire class held its breath, waiting to hear who had won the student council election.' Another student said that sentence was still rising action, not the climax yet. Using the definition of climax from the lesson, explain which student is correct and why.
choices: The first student is correct because the principal's entrance is a major moment and tension is highest here.
The second student is correct because the climax must come after the principal announces who won.
The first student is correct because everyone is holding their breath, which shows maximum stress in the story.
The second student is correct because the outcome is still unknown — nothing decisive has happened yet.
hints: Remember: the climax is not the sentence that feels most tense, but the sentence where something decisive actually happens.
Ask: has the outcome been decided in this sentence, or are the characters still waiting to find out?

problemText: Read this four-sentence story: 'Every morning, Diego fed his goldfish and watched it circle the tank. One day, he noticed the water looked cloudy and the fish was not swimming normally. Diego cleaned the entire tank, changed the water, and added medicine from the pet store. Two weeks later, his goldfish was healthy again, and Diego never missed a cleaning day after that.' A student sorted these sentences like this: Exposition (sentence 1), Rising Action (sentence 2), Climax (sentence 3), Resolution (sentence 4). Another student insisted that both sentences 2 and 3 should be labeled as rising action and climax together, not separately. Using the lesson's definition of plot stages, explain which student's sorting is correct and why, paying careful attention to where the outcome actually becomes decided.
choices: The second student is correct because sentence 2 continues building tension and the outcome is not decided until Diego's action in sentence 3.
The first student is correct because each of the four sentences represents exactly one distinct stage and together they cover the entire plot structure in order.
The first student is correct because the climax must always occur after rising action ends and sentence 3 shows the turning point moment.
The second student is correct because sentences 2 and 3 both describe the problem and its solution, which means they belong to the same stage of conflict.
hints: When does the outcome actually turn — when Diego notices the problem, or when he takes action to fix it?
Rising action keeps building tension while the outcome is still uncertain. Look at what sentence 2 does and what sentence 3 does.

problemText:
A character's response is what happens right after an event in a story. Which of the following is an example of a response that is SHOWN rather than told?

Consider this sentence: 'When Raj heard he didn't make the soccer team, he stared at the ground for five minutes without moving, then walked home alone instead of riding the bus with friends.'
choices: Raj stared at the ground for five minutes without moving and walked home alone
Raj felt disappointed because the rejection made him sad and let down by the outcome
Raj is sad and unhappy, which shows he is dealing with the pain of rejection
Raj was upset and discouraged, experiencing negative emotions about not making the team
hints: A shown response uses actions and behaviors you can see, not feeling words.
Look for what the character actually did or said, not a label someone gives him.

problemText:
Read the passage, then identify what event causes the character's response.

'When Devon opened the garage door, she found her entire bicycle project scattered across the floor—the frame, wheels, and gears in separate piles. She took a deep breath, grabbed a notebook, and started writing down each part's location and what she'd need to do next.'
choices: Devon takes a deep breath to calm herself down
The bicycle project is scattered across the floor
Devon writes down each part's location and makes a plan
Devon's bicycle needs to be rebuilt and put back together
hints: The event is the thing that happens first, before Devon does anything in response.
Look for what provokes or causes Devon to take action.

problemText:
A story includes this sentence: 'After the substitute teacher cancelled recess, Maya is resilient and determined.' Then the text shows Maya sitting quietly at her desk, working through extra math problems without complaining.

Which statement correctly compares what the text claims about Maya to what it actually shows?
choices: The text tells us Maya is resilient with a label but shows her sitting and working without complaining, which demonstrates actual resilience
The text only claims Maya is resilient in words, but does not show her doing anything brave or determined
The text claims Maya is resilient and determined, and shows her working through problems without complaining, which is actual evidence of that trait
The text proves Maya feels upset about losing recess by describing her working hard
hints: A claimed trait is a label someone gives a character. Evidence is what the character actually does.
Look for whether the character's actions match what the text says about them.

problemText:
Read this story passage:

'At the start of volleyball camp, Zara volunteered to be scorer and stayed on the sidelines the whole first week, asking the coaches questions about rules. When another player got injured in the second week, Zara jumped in to fill the position and made three successful serves before the end of practice. For the final tournament, Zara joined the starting lineup and played every set without hesitation.'

Which choice correctly describes both a response to a single event AND a lasting change that goes beyond that single event?
choices: Zara stops asking questions about rules and becomes a better player
Zara is confident and brave throughout the entire camp
Zara responds by making three successful serves when the other player gets injured
Zara responds to the injured player by jumping in to play, and she changes from staying on the sidelines to playing in the tournament
hints: A response happens right after one event. A change requires comparing what she does at the start to what she does at the end.
Make sure your answer points to something that happens near the beginning and something different that still happens near the end.

problemText:
Two students described the same character. Student 1 wrote: 'When Owen's robot broke during the competition, he threw the pieces across the gym.' Student 2 wrote: 'Owen responds to his robot breaking by throwing the pieces instead of asking for help to fix it.'

Which statement best explains why Student 2's description is more complete for the purpose of identifying a response?
choices: Student 2 names the event that provoked the response, while Student 1 only describes what Owen did
Student 2 explains Owen's response as a choice between two options, while Student 1 just reports an action without context
Student 2 shows what caused Owen to act, while Student 1 leaves out why the action matters
Student 1 forgot to mention that it was a competition
hints: Every response needs three parts: the event, what the character does, and how those two connect.
Student 1's sentence tells you the action but not why it matters or what caused it.

problemText:
Read this multi-part story:

'In chapter 2, after Diego's presentation was rejected by the panel, he packed his poster tube slowly, said 'Thanks for listening,' and left the room before anyone could speak. In chapter 5, when the same panel asked Diego to try again with a new idea, he started talking before they finished their invitation, showed them his sketches on his phone, and asked them three questions about their feedback.

Diego's teacher wrote: 'Diego is confident and takes criticism well.' A classmate wrote: 'Diego responds to rejection by leaving quickly, but changes to speaking up eagerly when given a second chance.'

Which analysis avoids claiming a trait without evidence and instead describes what actually changes from the first moment to the second?
choices: The teacher's analysis, because it identifies positive traits that Diego gains from the experience of rejection
The classmate's analysis, because it names the actual event in each moment and points to different behaviors at two different times
Both analyses are equally good because they both describe Diego's personality and how he grows from the two different events
Neither analysis works because Diego's actions in chapter 5 prove he was never actually rejected by the panel
hints: A trait like 'confident' is a claim. An actual change compares what a character does at one point to what they do at another point.
Look for which analysis points to specific moments in the text and shows how the character is acting differently by the end.
